To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PPs induce liver tumours in rodents and humans, but the mechanism is still unclear.

PPs are a group of compounds with different structures that bind and activate the PPARalpha, a transcription factor involved in lipid homeoestasis; the activation of the PPARalpha is species dependent; the long term administration of some PPs in rodent induces liver cancer; the human health risks of PPs are not well understood.
PPARalpha is a nuclear hormone receptor that binds to DNA in the form of a heterodimer with RXRalpha.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular mechanisms underlying the carcinogenic effects of PPs in rodents and the possible extrapolation to human health.
the study of the molecular mechanisms involved in the hepatocarcinogenic process and with the evaluation of the human health risk associated to the use of these drugs.

the study of the molecular mechanisms of PPARalpha action, with the identification of the molecular pathways that are involved in the development of liver tumors, as well as with the identification of new biomarkers of the liver carcinogenesis induced by PPs.

PPs, when used in human care, are not carcinogenic and that the risk assessment for the use of PPARalpha agonists in humans is based on the knowledge of the mechanisms of action of the PPARalpha and on the knowledge of human physiology.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the human health risk assessment for PPs should consider the different species and the different experimental conditions used for the evaluation of the carcinogenic effects of PPs, in order to avoid the misinterpretation of data.

the human health risks of PPs should be considered with caution and the risk/benefits should be balanced.

the human health risks of PPs are still uncertain and more research is necessary to clarify the issue.
